Welcome to Quackford City.

In this world, a punctuation mark is a traffic signal, a new word is a clue, and every reading task brings us closer to solving a mystery. Detective Duck makes literacy practice feel like an adventure worth coming back to.

An invitation to investigate

The Golden Quill has disappeared.

Yesterday afternoon, the famous Golden Quill disappeared from the Quackford Museum. A black feather was found near its glass cabinet. Muddy footprints led into the garden. Who might know the truth?

Meet Professor Puddle, Lily Lark, Benny Beaver and Mr. Crow. Each has a story. Young detectives must read, ask, listen and think before pointing a finger.

Evidence card

“Every clue is hiding in the words. I must read carefully.”

— Detective Duck, opening scene

Reading mission

Four obstacles. One gentle adventure.

📖

Vocabulary gaps

Unknown words can interrupt understanding and confidence.

🎙️

Slow or non-fluent reading

Oral reading can become hesitant when pronunciation and word recognition are difficult.

❗

Punctuation overlooked

Pupils may read without pausing at commas or full stops.

🗂️

Retelling the story

Sequencing events and connecting evidence may be difficult.

These are the reading needs highlighted in the submitted TSLB3402 blueprint, not newly collected site-level assessment data.

The mystery of the missing Golden Quill

Read the opening case, meet six original hand-drawn characters and explore the clues before playing.

A rainy morning. A curious case.
Official case report

Read the evidence.

Yesterday afternoon, the famous Golden Quill disappeared from the Quackford Museum.

It was kept in a glass cabinet in the main room.

At four o'clock, the guard locked the door.

At half past four, a visitor named Crow ran out of the room.

A black feather lay by the cabinet.

Muddy footprints led to the garden.

Detective's question

What makes a strong conclusion?

A careful detective does not guess. Pupils name a suspect, select relevant clues and explain their thinking using sentences such as:

“I think ____ because the evidence shows ____.”

Talk about the difference between a clue and proof.

The innovation dossier · TSLB3402

Why Detective Duck?

A reading-first digital intervention for Malaysian Year 3 English learners, rooted in learner difficulties identified in the submitted blueprint.

Where curiosity meets a clear learning goal.
1 · Identification of learner needs

The reading problem we are trying to solve

The blueprint identifies four intertwined challenges: limited vocabulary, slow and non-fluent reading, insufficient attention to punctuation, and difficulty comprehending or retelling a text. The focus is a lower-primary learner, particularly Year 3, before progression to upper primary.

Reading challengeNeed or gapGame response
Vocabulary deficitPupils struggle with unfamiliar words and their meanings in context.Magnifying Glass Case Dictionary: simple explanations, visuals and listening support.
Slow oral readingHesitation and uncertain pronunciation may reduce fluency.Read-aloud model and optional browser speech recognition or manual practice.
Ignoring punctuationReading may continue without meaningful pauses.Visual red-stop and yellow-slow punctuation checkpoints.
Weak retellingPupils have difficulty organising events and explaining what happened.Case Timeline, witness questions and written detective reasoning.

Source basis: the submitted innovation blueprint’s sections 1.0, 2.1 and 3.0. It cites academic research and observations; this site does not imply that a new baseline study has already been completed.

2 · Curriculum intent

Reading standards at the centre

KSSR English Year 3
3.2

Understand texts using reading strategies

The blueprint identifies this Content Standard as a basis for contextual vocabulary, strategies and comprehension.

KSSR English Year 3
3.3

Read fiction and non-fiction with enjoyment

The blueprint positions an immersive story and confidence-building practice as ways to encourage reading.

Standard wording above is a concise explanation of what the blueprint cites; refer to the applicable official DSKP for the exact full wording and relevant Learning Standards before preparing an assessed RPH. Academy speaking, listening, writing and Language Arts tasks are complementary extensions.
3 · Ideas and selection of tools

Why a detective game, not another worksheet?

Compared with Google Read Along

The blueprint values text-to-speech and speech recognition practice, but identifies the need for explicit punctuation and sequencing support in one connected narrative.

Compared with Seesaw

The blueprint recognises interactive activities while noting subscription-related constraints. Detective Duck uses a self-contained case experience and a locally playable HTML prototype.

Approach: role-play through a mystery, multisensory scaffolding, graded tasks, voluntary retries and positive badges. The blueprint discusses SCAMPER and the motivational role of autonomy and competence.
4 · Design alignment

Every mechanic has a purpose.

01

Make words visible

Contextual vocabulary pop-ups and accessible definitions.

02

Make pauses meaningful

Timed punctuation cues support expressive reading.

03

Make speech safe

Modelled reading, optional ASR, encouragement and retry.

04

Make retelling tangible

Sequence clues, talk to suspects and justify choices.

05

Make progress rewarding

Stars, rank names and badge collecting.

06

Make learning personal

Custom avatars, pupil-authored text and post-activity diary.

Implementation transparency

What the current HTML actually does

Confirmed functionality: the prototype includes case text, visual vocabulary, speech synthesis where available, punctuation cues, ordering tasks, feedback, saved game elements, avatar creation, a diary and additional mini-games.

Important boundaries: browser speech recognition can compare transcribed words, but it is not a validated phoneme-by-phoneme pronunciation assessment. The HTML does not by itself provide a cloud student database. Optional clubhouse pairing is not a moderated public multiplayer platform. Offline use of all features and browser permissions can differ by device.

These distinctions keep the portfolio accurate and guide a fair prototype evaluation.

A small field guide for educators

Teaching with Detective Duck

A flexible lesson route, classroom differentiation, formative assessment suggestions and learner-safe operating notes.

Before entering Quackford

Lesson intention

Audience: Year 3 primary ESL learners (the blueprint targets CEFR A1 Mid).

Core focus: recognising useful words, reading aloud with punctuation, understanding narrative events and retelling the case.

Possible lesson goal: By the end of the learning experience, pupils identify important story vocabulary, read selected sentences with appropriate pauses and sequence five events with support.

Suggested activity objective, not a claim that all pupils have met it.

Case kit

Before class

Use headphones where possible, check Chrome or another supported browser, consider a pair-work alternative if microphones are restricted and prepare a paper answer sheet for pupils who cannot access the game independently.

Explain that diary entries and avatar names are saved on the device; pupils should use nicknames rather than personal information.

Suggested sequence

One lesson · five learning moments

1
Hook · The missing Golden Quill (5 minutes)

Show the museum scene; ask pupils to predict what happened using simple English.

2
Vocabulary · Find the clues (10 minutes)

Pupils tap highlighted words, listen to models, and practise short meanings in pairs.

3
Fluency · Read with the signs (10 minutes)

Read the case file using yellow commas and red full-stop cues. Model first, then use partner reading.

4
Comprehension · Rebuild the timeline (10 minutes)

Pupils order event cards and compare their thinking before selecting the suspect.

5
Output & reflection (15 minutes)

Pupils write their detective explanation, receive formative feedback and complete “Today I learnt…” in the diary.

Suggested 50-minute example; adapt timing and task difficulty to your classroom.

Differentiation

Three ways to support every reader

Support

Read together

Use word pictures, teacher read-aloud, sentence frames and a peer. Allow oral responses where suitable.

Core

Investigate with a partner

Read, select evidence and sequence the case using the game prompts. Write a simple supported explanation.

Extension

Be the chief detective

Challenge evidence reliability, write extra descriptive sentences and create a comic or alternative ending.

Read-AloudPupil reads sentences with increasing confidence and reasonable phrasing.Short pre/post recording with consent or teacher rubric.
Timeline and interviewsPupil orders events and uses relevant evidence.5-event sequencing record / discussion notes.

Prototype development · evidence collection

Test the prototype, then tell its story honestly.

The checklist requires respondents, a testing location, a feedback method and an account of improvements. This page provides a pilot plan and editable local records, with no invented participant results.

Trial status: No verified classroom trial results, respondent numbers, dates, survey totals or before/after scores were provided in the uploaded files. The fields below are intentionally blank and must be completed after real testing.
Prototype development

A practical pilot plan

👥

Who can test?

Target Year 3 English learners with appropriate permissions, plus a small group of teachers or TESL classmates for usability review.

🏫

Where?

Classroom, language lab or supervised online session. Record the actual location and device conditions.

📋

How?

Teacher observation, short pupil smiley survey, task completion notes, and optional pre/post reading checks.

Pilot assessment tools

Use consistent indicators

IndicatorBefore trialAfter trialInterpretation
Target vocabulary (0–8)Number of target meanings recognisedRepeat comparable vocabulary checkDifference in correct responses
Punctuation reading (0–4)Pauses at four selected marksRepeat with comparable sentencesImproved pause awareness
Event order (0–5)Five story events sequencedRepeat / alternate textImproved narrative comprehension
Reading confidence (1–5)Smiley or simple self-ratingRepeat self-ratingPerceived comfort — not accuracy proof

These instruments are suggested for the trial; the submitted blueprint describes intended features but contains no completed experimental dataset.

Pupil exit ticket

Ask pupils to select a face or answer aloud:

1. Did you enjoy finding the clues? 😊 🙂 😐

2. Which new word do you remember?

3. What helped you read slowly or pause?

4. What was tricky?

5. What would make the game better?

Teacher observation prompts

1. Could pupils navigate independently?

2. Which support reduced hesitation?

3. Did pupils pause at the target marks?

4. Were the spoken instructions clear?

5. Which screen, device or task caused confusion?

Optional Google Forms

Gather classroom feedback in one place

For real multi-respondent data, create your own Google Form using the five pupil questions and teacher prompts above. Turn off email collection if it is not necessary, follow school consent policy and embed the published Form into the finished Google Site.

Suggested reporting: number of respondents, distribution of responses, themes in comments, examples of observed task barriers and changes made afterwards.

Reflection & improvement · learning from use

The next chapter is written after the trial.

What worked? What confused pupils? What changed because of the evidence? This section keeps the prototype design and future evaluation separate.

Design iteration

From a reading intervention to a richer Detective Academy

I
Original core concept

The Golden Quill mystery joins a word dictionary, oral reading support, punctuation cues, story sequencing and detective badges — the core elements described in the blueprint.

II
Expanded language practice

The uploaded current HTML adds four-skills and Language Arts activities such as Punctuation Fixer, Wiretap Alibi, Wanted Poster and Comic Strip Alibi.

III
Personalisation and reflection

The current game includes name and animal-avatar customisation plus a Detective Diary for “I learnt”, “I found difficult” and “Next time I will”.

IV
Extra play modes

Quack Dash provides an arcade literacy challenge, while the Quackford Detective Club offers friendly NPC/social-language stations with an optional experimental pairing feature.

V
Pilot → analysis → revision (pending)

After a supervised trial, compare the evidence and document actual changes. Do not claim impact or feedback before it is collected.

Checklist-based reflection

Three questions that matter

✅

Which need did it address?

Link each pupil response to vocabulary, fluency, punctuation or retelling.

📝

What did users tell us?

Report response numbers, observed patterns, direct quotes only with consent, and representative examples.

🔧

What did we improve?

Name the feature, the change and the reason. Retest to see whether the issue improves.

Professional learning

What to investigate next

Check usability with low-bandwidth devices, whether visual cues improve reading pauses, whether pupils can retell independently, and how helpful the feedback feels to different learners.

A future version could add secure teacher dashboards, stronger offline voice support and validated assessment rubrics if a suitable hosting/privacy model is established.

Public sharing and technical integrity

A few important notes

Keep student identification numbers, identity-card numbers and personal contact numbers out of the published Google Site. The blueprint’s cover sheet contains private fields and should not be published as a full document.

The game stores some user choices locally in the browser. Its optional speech-recognition feature depends on browser support and user permission. The optional two-player clubhouse connection is experimental; do not represent it as school-safe public multiplayer.

The website and the original game remain separate editable deliverables; the website prototype can be publicly hosted and linked from Google Sites, subject to your institution’s requirements.
